colloquial

/kuh-LOH-kwee-ul/ - the stress falls on LOH · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Colloquial means characteristic of informal, everyday conversation.

The coach's interviews are cheerfully colloquial — 'we got out-hustled, plain and simple' — and the beat writers quote him word for word.

Example

Translating her grandmother's letters, Mai kept the colloquial endearments as they were — 'little rice grain,' 'walk slowly now' — because scrubbing them into formal English would have lost the everyday voice that made the letters hers.

Colloquial describes register, not correctness: colloquial wording is what relaxed conversation sounds like, and it is wrong only where the setting demands formality. It is also broader than slang — 'kids' is colloquial and universal, while true slang belongs to an in-group and dates fast.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

conversational: Conversational describes anything pitched like everyday talk — a tone, a pace, an easy back-and-forth between speakers. Colloquial is the sharper label: it marks the particular words and phrasings that belong to informal speech itself, so a tone can be conversational while a single word is colloquial.

folksy: Folksy is homespun and familiar on purpose — a rocking-chair warmth that can shade into performance, as when a politician plays up small-town charm. Colloquial carries no such act: it simply names wording that belongs to ordinary, everyday conversation, with no performance implied.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

stilted: stiff and unnatural from too much formality

starchy: formal to the point of feeling ironed flat

Where it sits · how far speech drifts from the standard

relaxed → colloquial → slangy

relaxed vs. colloquial: Relaxed is milder than colloquial — a relaxed tone loosens the collar a little, while colloquial wording belongs fully to everyday speech.

slangy vs. colloquial: Slangy goes further than colloquial: colloquial phrasing is everyday language nearly everyone shares, while slangy expressions belong to an in-group and can shut outsiders out.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — col-: together (Latin com-, softened before l)

Root — loqu-: to speak (Latin loqui)

Suffix — -ial: adjective: of or like

Put it together: Col- (together) + loqu- (speak) + -ial = of speaking together. Latin colloquium was a talking-together, a conversation — and colloquial still means language with conversation's fingerprints on it.

Use the root in a new word: soliloquy: Half the class groaned when the teacher assigned Hamlet's longest soliloquy to memorize by Friday.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral

Colloquial is the neutral, precise label for everyday spoken wording — use it when 'informal' feels vague and 'slangy' overshoots. In a lab report or a court filing, colloquial phrasing is the thing to flag; over the dinner table, it is simply how people talk.
